title: How Much the Motors Can Give: Torque Limits and Heat in an Arm, the Payload That Fits at a Pose, and the Fastest a Move Can Be Made and Repeated

questions.question: What are the two torque limits of a motor?
options: The stall torque and the no load torque
The peak, for an instant, and the continuous, for ever without overheating
The motor's and the gear's
The torque at rest and the torque at speed
questions.explanation: A motor can give its peak briefly and its continuous torque indefinitely. Anything between is allowed for a time, which the winding's heat decides.

questions.question: A joint holding the arm stretched out reached its limit in:
options: 293 s, and folded in 2930 s
293 s, and folded it never did
Never, stretched out or folded
questions.explanation: 37.7 N m at the shoulder heats the winding past its limit in under five minutes. Folded, it needs 2.1 N m and settles below the limit.

questions.question: The payload at the tool with the arm out and folded was:
options: 2.50 kg and 10.00 kg
10.00 kg and 2.50 kg
10.00 kg in both, the structure's rating
2.50 kg in both
questions.explanation: Stretched out the arm's own weight uses most of the continuous torque. Folded, the joints had room for more than the structure's 10 kg rating.

questions.question: A move of 0.7 rad by the peak limits and by the continuous limits took:
options: 0.29 s by both
questions.explanation: The peak torque allows a faster move than the heat does. The rms over the move has to stay inside the continuous limit.

questions.question: Why can a move be fine once and not all day?
options: The rms heat accumulates: 118 K steady with no wait against 27 K with a wait of 4 s
The gears wear a little on each move
The battery sags as the day goes on
The bus rate falls when the servos are warm
questions.explanation: Each move leaves heat behind. With no wait the winding settled 118 K up, over its 75 K limit; with 4 s between moves, 27 K.

questions.question: How does the inertia part of the torque change as a move is made faster?
options: In proportion to one over the duration
Not at all: only the weight matters
As the inverse cube of the duration
As the inverse square of the duration: halving it asked 4.0 times
questions.explanation: Accelerations scale as one over the time squared. The part of the torque that holds the weight is the same however fast the move.
